title: What is fasting glucose and why does it matter? | Levels | Levels
abstract:
## Why should I check fasting glucose?  
Fasting glucose is a valuable measurement because it assesses the health of your body’s systems for maintaining[its ideal baseline level](https://www.levels.com/blog/what-is-glucose). If your fasting blood glucose level is high, it’s an indication that something in the process is not working correctly, and that can have serious downstream consequences.  
An elevated fasting blood sugar level is related to[8 of the top 10 leading causes of death](https://www.levels.com/blog/leading-causes-of-death-high-blood-sugar), and yet many people without a diagnosed metabolic condition pay little attention to it. Most people with a prediabetic amount of glucose[don’t even know it](https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/pdfs/data/statistics/national-diabetes-statistics-report.pdf).
When you eat and take in excess glucose, your pancreas releases a hormone called insulin, which helps clear it from your bloodstream into cells or storage. But if you consistently spike your glucose levels with high-glycemic foods, for example, your body has to produce large surges of insulin to deal with it. Over time, this can cause insulin resistance—a condition in which your cells become less sensitive to the hormone. Insulin resistance can factor into chronic conditions such as[heart disease](https://europepmc.org/article/med/8883497),[kidney disease](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajprenal.00340.2016), [diabetes](https://diabetes.diabetesjournals.org/content/61/4/778),[infertility](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3877124/), and[Alzheimer’s disease](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6277874). Insulin resistance can progress further to Type 2 diabetes mellitus, a condition in which your body is unable to adequately regulate blood sugar.
## What is the optimal range for fasting glucose?  
Since the late 90s, major medical groups like the [American Diabetes Association](https://diabetes.org/about-diabetes/diagnosis) (ADA) have recommended the following clinical guidelines for a diagnosis of diabetes:  
- **Clinically “normal” fasting glucose**: Less than 100 mg/dL
- **Prediabetes**: 100-125 mg/dL
- **Diabetes**: 126 mg/dL or higher  
These standards were based on clinical diabetes studies as well as broad population research showing that the majority of people fall under that 100 mg/dL threshold. But what’s “normal” in the US population may still be unhealthy.  
Many subsequent studies have found that people at the upper end of the normal range (i.e. 85-99 mg/dL) still experience serious health consequences, such as heightened[stroke](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3329666/),[cardiovascular disease](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4934381/), [heart attack](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3687304/#:~:text=As%20fasting%20glucose%20levels%20increased,for%20hemorrhagic%20stroke%20did%20not.), and[diabetes](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa050080) risk.  
**Based on this research, Levels suggests that 100 mg/dL still appears too high for healthy metabolism. Instead,we recommend a fasting glucose level of72-85 mg/dL.**
